chunk-001:c006.proposition: Physical science cannot explain qualitative conscious experience while its descriptive vocabulary remains exclusively quantitative.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: Neuroscientific correlations between brain activity and experience require a philosophical theory explaining why those correlations obtain.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-01.proposition: Strong emergence requires fundamental psychophysical laws and consequently resembles dualism, unlike weak emergence under existing physical laws.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-04.proposition: Dualism and strong emergence incur additional theoretical commitments, whereas panpsychism can avoid materialism's explanatory gap without the same cost.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-05.proposition: Because physics describes matter's behavior rather than its intrinsic nature, consciousness can constitute matter intrinsically without a supernatural addition.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: Treating consciousness as independent data, panpsychism parsimoniously unifies matter's quantitative properties with the qualitative reality of experience.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-09.proposition: Although the combination problem remains open, split-brain research and possible bridging principles provide routes from simple constituent experience to unified system-level consciousness.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c02.proposition: Panpsychism has no necessary religious implication, and treating consciousness as fundamental does not strengthen an inference from cosmic origins to God.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c03.proposition: Natural selection can shape simple forms of experience into increasingly complex mentality unless some specific human mental feature is shown to require more.

chunk-003:chunk-003-c07.proposition: Even if God exists, consciousness still requires an intelligible and parsimonious account of how it fits within the world.
